Include supports that remove practical barriers to work (affordable childcare, transportation, mental-health/addiction services) and incentive structures like wage-top-up credits or tax breaks for employers who hire and train program participants. Make funding outcomes-based so providers are rewarded for placing people in sustainable jobs, and allow local/community and faith-based organizations to run programs since they know needs best. Finally, build in gradual benefit tapering to avoid cliffs, require reasonable work-search or training participation, and evaluate programs regularly so ineffective ones are retooled. Which of those approaches do you think would be most politically and practically feasible?

llm_text: I’d build milestones that are measurable and time-bound so assistance is clearly a bridge, not a permanent lifeline. Pair this with wraparound help (childcare, transportation, case management) so people can meet goals, and carve out exemptions for the disabled, elderly, or primary caregivers. Offer positive incentives too — matched savings or small business/startup grants when milestones are met — so the system rewards initiative rather than replacing it.
